DEVICE.doc:
The terminal as the line editor uses it: the standard input and output,
put in raw mode and read key by key, the window's size, and how the
terminal measures what it draws.

`Device` is Rune's, over the Basis's `Terminal`: the runtime puts the
terminal back however the program ends, counts the window's changes of
size, and reads a console of Windows. `PosixDevice` is the same
signature over `Posix.TTY` and `OS.IO.poll` alone, for the other
compilers of Standard ML: it knows no size but `COLUMNS` and `LINES`,
sees no resize, and puts the terminal back at `leave` only.

members.name: available
members.doc:
`available ()` is whether the standard input and output are both a
terminal and `TERM` is not `dumb`: whether a program can edit there.

members.name: size
members.spec: val size : unit -> {columns : int, rows : int}
members.doc:
`size ()` is the columns and rows of the window, 80 and 24 where it
cannot be known.

members.name: resizes
members.doc:
`resizes ()` is how many times the window has changed its size since
the first call.

A program draws everything again when it has grown. It stays 0 where
changes cannot be seen.

members.name: enter
members.doc:
`enter {undo}` puts the terminal in raw mode: each byte as it is
typed, no echo, no signal from a key.

`undo` is what to write when it is put back, to take back what the
program turned on with escapes.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when the standard input is not a terminal.

members.name: quiet
members.doc:
`quiet ()` turns the echo off and leaves a return as it was typed,
and a signal key is a signal again.

Raw mode has taken the signals. `quiet` puts them back without
turning the echo on. It clears the undo text `enter` stored: the
caller writes that text first, since `leave` would otherwise write
it later.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when the standard input is not a terminal.

members.name: leave
members.doc: `leave ()` puts the terminal back as it was, writing `undo`.

members.name: read
members.spec: val read : Time.time option -> string option
members.doc:
`read wait` is the bytes typed, waiting at most `wait`, or `NONE` at
the end of the input.

`wait` `NONE` waits as long as it takes; `SOME ""` is nothing in the
time, or a resize that ended the wait.

**Raises** `OS.SysErr` when the read fails.

members.name: write
members.doc: `write s` writes `s` to the standard output at once.

members.name: policy
members.doc:
`policy ()` is how the terminal measures a grapheme cluster.

By code point in VS Code's terminal on Windows (`TERM_PROGRAM`),
which draws each code point of a cluster as wide as its own width,
and by cluster everywhere else.

EMULATOR.doc:
A terminal emulated in memory: what a screen shows after a program has
written to it, for testing what a program draws without a terminal.

It knows what a line editor writes: text, with grapheme clusters as wide
as the width policy says and a wide one wrapped whole; carriage return,
newline (which scrolls at the bottom), backspace and tab; ECMA-48's
cursor movements (CUU, CUD, CUF, CUB, CHA, CUP), erasing in a line and
in the display (EL, ED), and SGR; and xterm's pending wrap -- after a
character in the last column the cursor stays there until the next
character, which goes to the start of the next line. Modes are
recorded (bracketed paste, a hidden cursor); OSC titles/marks and other
control strings are consumed through their terminators across writes,
without putting their payload on screen. Other escapes are ignored.

members.name: cell
members.doc:
A cell of the screen: the cluster it shows (" " when blank, "" for
the right half of a wide cluster) and its style.

members.name: screen
members.doc: A screen and its cursor.

members.name: new
members.spec: val new : {columns : int, rows : int, policy : Grapheme.policy} -> screen
members.doc:
`new {columns, rows, policy}` is a blank screen of that size with the
cursor at its top left, measuring clusters by `policy`.

**Example** `cursor (new {columns = 80, rows = 24, policy = Grapheme.ByCluster}) = (0, 0)`

members.name: resize
members.spec: val resize : screen * {columns : int, rows : int} -> screen
members.doc:
`resize (s, size)` preserves the top-left cells, styles and modes at the new dimensions.

Cells past
the new right/bottom edges are clipped; text does not reflow. The cursor
is clamped and a wide cluster clipped in half is erased. Dimensions must
be positive (otherwise Size). A program can redraw after its resize.

members.name: write
members.doc:
`write (s, bytes)` is the screen after `bytes` were written to `s`.

Bytes of a UTF-8 character or an escape split between two writes
are joined, as a terminal joins them.

members.name: cursor
members.doc: `cursor s` is the cursor's row and column, from 0.

members.name: row
members.spec: val row : screen * int -> cell list
members.doc:
`row (s, i)` is the cells of row `i`, without the blank cells of
default style at its end.

**Raises** `Subscript` when there is no row `i`.

members.name: text
members.doc:
`text s` is the screen as text, a line a row, without the blanks at
the ends of rows and the empty rows at the end.

**Example** `text (write (new {columns = 4, rows = 2, policy = Grapheme.ByCluster}, "abcde")) = "abcd\ne"`

members.name: scrolled
members.doc: `scrolled s` is how many rows have scrolled off the top.

members.name: modes
members.spec: val modes : screen -> {bracketedPaste : bool, cursorVisible : bool}
members.doc:
`modes s` is whether bracketed paste is on (mode 2004) and whether
the cursor is shown (mode 25).

HISTORY.doc:
The history of what was typed at a prompt, kept in a file that several
sessions share.

An entry is one accepted input, however many lines it has; in the file
it is one line, with its newlines and backslashes escaped. Each entry
is appended with one write, so that two sessions that add at once
interleave entries and never lines, and a session reads at each prompt
what the others have appended since it last looked. An entry the same
as the one before it is not added again. The file is kept under twice
the limit of entries by writing the last of them to a new file and
renaming it over the old.

members.name: history
members.doc: A history: its entries, and the file they are kept in, if any.

members.name: defaultFile
members.doc:
`defaultFile ()` is where Rune's programs keep their history, or
`NONE` when the environment names no place.

It is `$XDG_STATE_HOME/rune/history`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\rune\history`
on Windows, or `~/.local/state/rune/history`, by the first of those
variables that is set.

members.name: load
members.spec: val load : {file : string option, limit : int} -> history
members.doc:
`load {file, limit}` is the history of `file`, its last `limit`
entries; an empty one when the file does not exist yet, and one that
is not kept when `file` is `NONE`.

members.name: entries
members.doc: `entries h` is the entries of `h`, the oldest first.

members.name: add
members.doc:
`add (h, e)` adds the entry `e` to `h` and its file, after what the
other sessions have added.

It does nothing when `e` is empty or is the last entry. A file that
cannot be written is left alone.

members.name: refresh
members.doc:
`refresh h` reads what other sessions have appended to the file since
`h` last read it.

members.name: escape
members.doc:
`escape e` is the entry `e` as a line of the file: a newline is `\n`,
a carriage return `\r`, a backslash `\\`.

**Example** `escape "a\nb\\c" = "a\\nb\\\\c"`

members.name: unescape
members.doc:
`unescape l` is the entry that the line `l` is.

**Law** `unescape (escape e) = e`

**Example** `unescape "a\\nb" = "a\nb"`

KEY.doc:
Keys: the bytes a terminal sends turned into the keys that were pressed.

A terminal sends a printable key as its UTF-8, a key with Ctrl as a
control character, a key with Alt as Escape and the key, and the
arrows, the function keys and the rest as escape sequences: CSI
(`ESC [`, parameters, a final byte) or SS3 (`ESC O` and a byte), with
the modifiers in xterm's parameter. The decoder reads a CSI sequence to
its final byte before it looks it up, so that a sequence it does not
know is reported as `Unknown` and never typed as text. Bracketed paste
(mode 2004) arrives as one `Paste`. It also reads the kitty keyboard
protocol's `CSI code ; modifiers u` and xterm's `CSI 27 ; modifiers ; code ~`, where a terminal sends them.

Escape alone is ambiguous: it begins every sequence. The decoder keeps
it pending, and `flush` \-- called when no byte has come for a while, 50
ms by default in `LineEdit` \-- says it was the key Escape (or Alt and
`[` or `O`, when those followed it).

The decoder is a value: `feed` takes it and some bytes to the keys they
complete and the decoder that waits for the rest, so the bytes of one
key may come in any number of reads.

members.name: name
members.spec:
datatype name =
    Up | Down | Left | Right | Home | End | Insert | Delete | PageUp | PageDown
  | Enter | Tab | Backspace | Escape | F of int
members.doc: The keys that are not characters.

members.name: mods
members.spec: type mods = {shift : bool, alt : bool, ctrl : bool}
members.doc:
The modifiers held with a key. Shift is reported for the named keys
only: a character typed with Shift is the shifted character.

members.name: event
members.spec:
datatype event =
    Char of int * mods
  | Named of name * mods
  | Paste of string
  | CursorAt of int * int
  | Reply of string
  | Focus of bool
  | Unknown of string
members.doc:
What was pressed or sent.

`Char (c, m)` is the code point `c` with the modifiers `m`: Ctrl and
a letter is the lower-case letter with `ctrl` (Ctrl-A is `Char (97, ...)`), and the control characters that are not keys of their own are
`@`, `\`, `]`, `^` and `_` with `ctrl`. A byte that is not UTF-8 is
U+FFFD. `Named (n, m)` is a named key. `Paste s` is the text of a
bracketed paste, as it came. `CursorAt (row, column)` is a terminal's
report of its cursor (from 1), the answer to `ESC [ 6 n`. `Reply s` is
another answer to a question, an escape sequence with a private
parameter (`ESC [ ? ...`). `Focus b` is the window's focus gained or
lost (mode 1004). `Unknown s` is a sequence the decoder does not
know, as it came.

members.name: none
members.doc:
No modifier.

**Example** `none = {shift = false, alt = false, ctrl = false}`

members.name: decoder
members.doc: A decoder: the bytes of a key begun and not yet complete.

members.name: empty
members.doc:
The decoder that has seen nothing.

**Example** `pending empty = false`

members.name: feed
members.spec: val feed : decoder * string -> event list * decoder
members.doc:
`feed (d, s)` is the keys that `d`'s pending bytes and `s` complete,
in the order they were sent, and the decoder that holds what is left
of a key not complete.

The keys do not depend on how the bytes were split between calls:
tests/lib/terminal/key.sml checks that every split of many streams
gives the same keys.

**Example** `#1 (feed (empty, "a\027[A")) = [Char (97, none), Named (Up, none)]`

members.name: pending
members.doc: `pending d` is whether `d` holds the beginning of a key.

members.name: flush
members.spec: val flush : decoder -> event list * decoder
members.doc:
`flush d` is the keys that `d`'s pending bytes are when no more come,
and the empty decoder.

Escape alone is the key Escape, Escape and `[` or `O` is that
character with Alt, an incomplete sequence is `Unknown`, an
incomplete UTF-8 character U+FFFD.

**Example** `#1 (flush (#2 (feed (empty, "\027")))) = [Named (Escape, none)]`

members.name: toString
members.doc:
`toString e` is a key as Emacs writes one: `C-a`, `M-b`, `Up`,
`S-Tab`, `F5`, `SPC`, a character as itself; the other events by
their constructor and what they carry.

**Example** `toString (Char (97, {shift = false, alt = true, ctrl = true})) = "C-M-a"`

LINE_EDIT.doc:
A line editor: what is typed at a prompt, edited with Emacs's keys,
drawn on a terminal, of one line or many.

The editor is a pure core under a thin loop (docs/plans/repl.md, D7).
`step` takes a state and a key to the next state and what it asks of
the loop; `layout` turns a state into a frame, the rows of cells the
terminal should show and where the cursor is, wrapping by display
width itself; `diff` turns the frame the terminal shows and the next
into the bytes that change one into the other, with relative moves and
only the rows that changed. `readLine` is the loop: it reads keys,
steps and draws, and falls back to a basic mode -- a prompt and
`TextIO.inputLine` \-- where the terminal cannot be edited on.

The keys are readline's: Ctrl-A, Ctrl-E, Ctrl-B, Ctrl-F, Alt-B, Alt-F
and the arrows to move; Ctrl-D, Delete, Backspace, Ctrl-K, Ctrl-U,
Ctrl-W, Alt-D and Alt-Backspace to delete, killing into a ring that
Ctrl-Y and Alt-Y yank from; Ctrl-T, Alt-U, Alt-L and Alt-C; Ctrl-\_ to
undo; Up and Down through the lines and then the history, searching
it by what was typed; Ctrl-R to search it incrementally; Tab to
complete; Enter to accept a complete input or begin a new line, and
Alt-Enter for a new line always; Ctrl-L to clear the screen; Ctrl-C to
cancel; Ctrl-Z to suspend. `bindings` changes them.

With `keys = Vi` the editor has Vi's modes: what is typed is inserted,
as with Emacs's keys, until Escape, which goes to the normal mode,
where letters are commands -- counts, the motions h l w b e 0 ^ \$, the
operators d c y with a motion or doubled, x X D C s S r \~ p P u, j and
k through the lines and the history, G and gg, and i a I A o O back to
inserting. The cursor is a block in the normal mode and a bar while
inserting.

members.name: command
members.spec:
datatype command =
    Insert
  | BeginningOfLine | EndOfLine | ForwardChar | BackwardChar | ForwardWord | BackwardWord
  | PreviousLine | NextLine | PreviousHistory | NextHistory | BeginningOfHistory | EndOfHistory
  | BeginningOfBuffer | EndOfBuffer
  | DeleteChar | DeleteCharOrEnd | BackwardDeleteChar | KillLine | BackwardKillLine
  | KillWord | BackwardKillWord | KillWordBehind | Yank | YankPop
  | TransposeChars | UpcaseWord | DowncaseWord | CapitalizeWord | Undo
  | AcceptOrNewline | Newline | Complete | ReverseSearch | Abort | Cancel | ClearScreen | Suspend
  | Ignore
members.doc:
What a key does. `Insert` types the character of the key; the others
are named as in readline.

members.name: emacs
members.doc: Readline's keys, as the comment above lists them.

members.name: keys
members.doc:
Whether letters are typed always (Emacs's keys), or are Vi's commands
in its normal mode.

members.name: config
members.spec:
type config = {
  prompt : string, continuation : string,
  isComplete : string -> bool,
  complete : string * int -> {start : int, candidates : string list},
  hint : string -> string option,
  highlight : string -> (int * int * Style.style) list,
  styles : {prompt : Style.style, hint : Style.style, menu : Style.style, search : Style.style,
            control : Style.style, mark : Style.style},
  bindings : (Key.event * command) list,
  escapeTimeout : Time.time,
  policy : Grapheme.policy,
  basic : bool,
  keys : keys}
members.doc:
What the editor is given: the prompts, what it asks of the program,
its styles and keys.

`prompt` begins the first line and `continuation` the others. `isComplete text` says whether Enter
accepts `text` or begins a new line. `complete (text, i)` is where
the word before byte `i` begins and what it can be completed to.
`hint text` is text shown faintly after the end, which Right or
Ctrl-E there accepts. `highlight text` is styles for byte ranges of
the text, `(start, stop, style)`. `styles` are those of the parts the
editor draws itself. `escapeTimeout` is how long Escape waits for
the rest of a sequence; `policy` how the terminal measures clusters;
`basic` asks for the basic mode; `keys` whether Vi's modes are on
(`bindings` are those of both modes but the normal mode's letters).

members.name: defaults
members.doc:
A configuration for an input of one line at the prompt `"> "`.

Every input is complete; there is nothing to complete, hint or
highlight; hints are faint and a search bold; the keys are Emacs's,
Escape waits 50 ms, and clusters are measured whole.

members.name: state
members.doc:
What the editor holds: the text, the cursor, the kill ring, what can
be undone, the history and where in it the text came from, and Vi's
mode.

members.name: normal
members.doc: `normal s` is whether `s` is in Vi's normal mode.

members.name: outcome
members.spec: datatype outcome = Continue | Accept of string | Cancelled | EndOfInput | Clear | Stop
members.doc:
What a key asks of the loop: nothing more, to return the text or no
text, to clear the screen, or to suspend the process.

members.name: start
members.spec: val start : string vector * string -> state
members.doc:
`start (history, text)` is the state of a new input with `text`
typed and the cursor after it, `history` the entries Up goes back
through, the oldest first.

members.name: step
members.spec: val step : config * state * Key.event -> state * outcome
members.doc:
`step (c, s, e)` is the state after the key `e`, and what it asks.

**Example** `text (#1 (step (defaults, start (Vector.fromList [], ""), Key.Char (97, Key.none)))) = "a"`

members.name: text
members.doc: `text s` is the text, its lines joined by newlines.

members.name: cursor
members.doc: `cursor s` is the byte of the text the cursor is at.

members.name: cell
members.doc:
A cell of the screen: a cluster (" " blank, "" the right half of a
wide one) and its style, as the emulator has them.

members.name: frame
members.spec: type frame = {rows : cell list vector, cursor : int * int}
members.doc:
What the terminal shows of the editor: rows of cells, without the
blank cells of plain style at their ends, and the cursor's row and
column.

members.name: layout
members.spec: val layout : config * state * int -> frame
members.doc:
`layout (c, s, columns)` is the frame of `s` on a terminal that wide.

It holds the prompt, the lines wrapped at `columns`, the hint, the
matches of a completion and the line of a search.

members.name: diff
members.spec: val diff : {old : frame option, new : frame, columns : int, drawn : int} -> string * int
members.doc:
`diff {old, new, columns, drawn}` is the bytes that change what the
terminal shows from `old` to `new`, and the rows drawn on since.

`old` is `NONE` when nothing is drawn yet and the cursor is at the
start of an empty line; `drawn` is the rows drawn on before. Rows that
did not change are not written; a row is written from its first
changed cell; the cursor moves relative to where it was, by rows, and
to a column. Neither frame may be taller than the terminal.

tests/lib/terminal/edit.sml checks, for random edits at random
widths, that `Emulator` shows `new` once it has been given what
`diff` writes over a screen that shows `old`.

members.name: result
members.spec: datatype result = Line of string | Interrupted | End
members.doc:
What `readLine` read: a line, a cancelled one, or the end of the
input.

members.name: basic
members.doc:
`basic c` is whether `readLine` keeps to its basic mode with `c`, by
the rule `readLine` gives.

A program with a basic mode of its own, as the REPL has, asks it
before it reads.

members.name: keepRaw
members.doc:
`keepRaw`, when set, asks `readLine` to leave the terminal quiet
after an accepted line: the echo off, and Ctrl-C a signal.

The REPL sets it. Putting the terminal back would turn the echo on,
and a key typed before quiet mode would show up in what the code
writes. Full raw mode would instead take Ctrl-C as a byte. An
interrupt and the end of the input put the terminal back either way.

members.name: promptHook
members.doc:
`promptHook` is what to run once the terminal is raw, just before the
prompt is drawn.

members.name: beforePrompt
members.doc:
`beforePrompt`, when set, is run once the terminal is raw, just
before the prompt is drawn. The basic mode does not run it.

The REPL announces the prompt there. A key typed at that
announcement is then read as itself: in the cooked mode a return is
translated, and echoed, before the editor can see it.

members.name: readLine
members.spec: val readLine : config * History.history option -> result
members.doc:
`readLine (c, h)` reads an input at the terminal with the editor,
going back through the history `h` and adding the input to it.

It puts the terminal back before it returns, unless `keepRaw` is set
and it read a line, when the terminal stays quiet. Where `beforePrompt`
is set, it is called once the terminal is raw and just before the
prompt is drawn. The keys a read gave after the one that ended the
input -- typed ahead in the same burst, while the program was busy --
are not lost: the next `readLine` takes them before it reads. It is
the basic mode when `#basic c`, when the standard input or output is
not a terminal, when `TERM` is `dumb`, `unknown`, `cons25` or
`emacs`, when `INSIDE_EMACS` names comint, or when `RUNE_BASIC_REPL`
is set.

members.name: terminal
members.spec: val terminal : unit -> {policy : Grapheme.policy option, kitty : bool}
members.doc:
`terminal ()` is what the terminal said of itself at the first
`readLine`, once its answers have come.

How it measures a cluster, which `readLine` then uses in place of the
config's `policy`, and whether it speaks the kitty keyboard protocol,
which `readLine` turns on while it reads (keys told apart: Escape at
once, Ctrl-I apart from Tab). `NONE` and false where it has not
answered.

STYLE.doc:
The look of text on a terminal: colours and attributes, the escapes of
ECMA-48's SGR that give them, and whether a program should use them at
all.

A style is a record, so that a cell of a screen can carry one and two
can be compared; `sgr` writes the escape that sets a style from nothing,
and `change` the shortest that goes from one style to another. A colour
is one of the terminal's 16, which follow the user's theme, one of 256,
or a colour of 24 bits; `downgrade` maps one a terminal does not have
to the nearest it has.

members.name: color
members.spec: datatype color = Default | Ansi of int | Indexed of int | Rgb of int * int * int
members.doc:
A colour: the terminal's own, one of its 16 or of xterm's 256, or one
of 24 bits.

`Ansi` is 0 to 7 and their bright forms 8 to 15; `Rgb` is red, green
and blue of 0 to 255.

members.name: style
members.spec:
type style = {fg : color, bg : color, bold : bool, faint : bool, italic : bool,
              underline : bool, reverse : bool, struck : bool}
members.doc:
A style: the colours of the text and of its background, and the
attributes.

members.name: plain
members.doc:
The style of plain text: default colours, no attribute.

**Example** `sgr plain = "\027[0m"`

members.name: sgr
members.doc:
`sgr s` is the escape that sets `s` whatever the terminal had before:
a reset and then the parameters of `s`.

**Example** `sgr {fg = Ansi 1, bg = Default, bold = true, faint = false, italic = false, underline = false, reverse = false, struck = false} = "\027[0;1;31m"`

members.name: change
members.doc:
`change (a, b)` is what to write to go from style `a` to style `b`:
nothing when they are the same, else `sgr b`.

**Example** `change (plain, plain) = ""`

members.name: parameters
members.doc:
`parameters p` is the style that the SGR parameters `p` set from
plain.

They are written as in an escape or a `GCC_COLORS` value ("1;31",
"38;5;203", "38;2;255;95;95"); parameters it does not know are left
out, and so is everything after a part that is not a number.

**Example** `#bold (parameters "1;31") andalso #fg (parameters "1;31") = Ansi 1`

members.name: depth
members.spec: datatype depth = Mono | Colors16 | Colors256 | TrueColor
members.doc:
How many colours a terminal shows: none (attributes only), 16, 256,
or 24 bits.

members.name: depth
members.doc:
`depth ()` is the colours the environment says the terminal has.

`Mono` when `NO_COLOR` is set and not empty, `TrueColor` when
`COLORTERM` is `truecolor` or `24bit`, 256 when `TERM` ends in
`256color`, else 16.

members.name: downgrade
members.doc:
`downgrade d s` is `s` with each colour that `d` lacks replaced by the
nearest one it has.

An `Rgb` becomes the nearest of the 256, one of the 256 the nearest of
the 16, and every colour `Default` at `Mono`.

**Example** `#fg (downgrade Colors256 (parameters "38;2;255;0;0")) = Indexed 196`

members.name: choice
members.doc: When to style: always, never, or when the stream is a terminal.

members.name: enabled
members.doc:
`enabled (c, isTerminal)` is whether a program should style a stream,
`isTerminal` saying whether the stream is a terminal.

For `Auto` it is the rule of Rune's compiler (docs/diagnostics.md):
`NO_COLOR`, `FORCE_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, `CLICOLOR` and `TERM`
decide before `isTerminal` does.

**Example** `enabled (Never, true) = false`
